claims.text: The patient presented on 2026-01-07 with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset following physical exertion, characterized as throbbing and diffuse with associated mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines, though the patient's mother has type 2 diabetes and father has hypertension.

Initial triage and examination on 2026-01-07 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examinations on 2026-01-07 were unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, intact motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 2026-01-07 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 2026-01-07 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L) and a CRP of 8 mg/L, with normal renal and liver function tests.
On 2026-01-07, the patient was diagnosed with Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and admitted to the Neurology ward.
On 2026-01-07, the treatment plan included starting oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and arranging MRI/MRA of the brain and cerebral vasculature for that evening.

On 2026-01-07, the patient reported persistent headache rated 7/10, with blood pressure recorded at 150/92 mmHg and new laboratory findings of mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 2026-01-07, the plan was to continue nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours and add oral potassium chloride 1 g twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
On 2026-01-07 at 20:00, the patient's GP was contacted to provide an update on the admission and preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 2026-01-08, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, and CRP remained at 12 mg/L with persistent mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L).
On 2026-01-08, the medication regimen was adjusted to nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, with a plan to repeat MRA in 48 hours and continue potassium chloride 1 g twice daily.
On 2026-01-08, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, and medications like triptans or ergotamines.
On 2026-01-09, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 3/10, with new laboratory findings of mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L) and blood pressure of 125/80 mmHg.
On 2026-01-09, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 2026-01-09, the rehab team assessed the patient, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.

On 2026-01-10, the patient reported headache intensity of 2/10, with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, and the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and continue dietary management for hyponatremia.
On 2026-01-10, a repeat MRA was planned for 2026-01-11, and the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management and lifestyle modifications.
On 2026-01-11, the patient reported headache intensity of 2/10 with blood pressure 125/78 mmHg, and the plan was to perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-11 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS, and discharge planning was initiated for 2026-01-12.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches, with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and was deemed fit for discharge.

The discharge plan on 2026-01-12 included continuing nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks, and advice to avoid known triggers.
On 2026-01-12 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss the hospital stay, diagnosis, and discharge medication, which was documented as amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 documents amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
